title: Kontorovich–Nakamura crystallographic packings ↔ ES integral geometry
connection: Kontorovich–Nakamura classify crystallographic sphere packings via integral Lorentzian reflective lattices; ES has lattice/quaternion reformulations and a cubic integral surface.
why: Packing local-global problems (Apollonian) are the main family with proved reciprocity obstructions akin to T1.
first_step: Check whether any ES lattice L_ρ (LATTICE_MEETING.md) is a reflective Lorentzian lattice.
refs: Kontorovich–Nakamura, Geometry and arithmetic of crystallographic sphere packings, PNAS 116 (2019)

title: Discretised projection (Bourgain) / Furstenberg sets (Ren–Wang) for p-adic or real ES geometry
connection: Bourgain's discretised projection theorem and Ren–Wang's Furstenberg set resolution give sum-product in ℝ at scale δ; ES solution ratios (x:y:z) live on a real curve family.
why: Could bound concentration of solution directions, relevant to size-window (FORCED_WINDOW) statements.
first_step: Express the set of normalized ES solutions (x/n, y/n, z/n) as a δ-discretised set and test projection-dimension statistics numerically.
refs: Ren–Wang, Furstenberg sets estimate in the plane, arXiv:2308.08819
Bourgain, The discretized sum-product and projection theorems, J. Anal. Math. 112 (2010)

title: Type II as SL₂(ℤ) matrices with prescribed off-diagonal product (hyperbolic lattice counting)
connection: ff′ − ab = 1 with ab = 4c²dp: Type II certificates are integer matrices of determinant 1 with diagonal ≡ −1 (mod 4cd) and off-diagonal product fixed — a hyperbolic lattice-point problem in Γ(4cd)-cosets.
why: Spectral counting in congruence subgroups (Selberg 3/16, Kim–Sarnak 7/64) applies; the fixed product ab is a 'divisor-split' constraint.
first_step: Count matrices in a coset of Γ(4cd) with |entries| ≤ T and ab = 4c²dp numerically, compare with the spectral main term.
refs: Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms (2002)
Kim–Sarnak, appendix to Kim, Functoriality for the exterior square of GL4…, JAMS 16 (2003)

title: Blomer–Harcos hybrid subconvexity for effective ternary representations
connection: Blomer–Harcos give hybrid subconvexity for twisted L-functions, enabling effective representation results for ternary forms (with Siegel caveats); ES's ternary analogues would need such input.
why: Effective bounds combined with 10^18 verification are the only way a ternary route could close a range.
first_step: Quantify the size beyond which Blomer–Harcos yields representations, for the discriminants arising in any ES ternary reformulation.
refs: Blomer–Harcos, Hybrid bounds for twisted L-functions, J. reine angew. Math. 621 (2008)

title: Siegel–Rogers mean value / random-lattice model for ES lattices L_ρ
connection: Siegel's mean value theorem and Rogers' higher moments give the distribution of lattice-point counts in random lattices; ES(p) ⟺ some lattice L_ρ(p) has a vector in a cone (LATTICE_MEETING).
why: A random-lattice model predicts P(no vector in cone) and its p-dependence — a cleaner heuristic than divisor lotteries.
first_step: Compute covolume and cone volume for L_ρ(p) and compare empirical 'empty cone' frequency with Rogers' Poisson prediction.
refs: Rogers, Mean values over the space of lattices, Acta Math. 94 (1955)

title: Hyperbolic circle problem in Γ₀(N) for e-slice counts
connection: Counting Γ₀(N)-orbit points in hyperbolic discs has spectral asymptotics with error controlled by exceptional eigenvalues; e-slice certificates ab | N with a ≡ −b (mod e) can be phrased via matrices with lower-left entry divisible by e.
why: Moves the e-slice count into a standard spectral counting problem.
first_step: Construct the matrix encoding of e-slice certificates and count numerically vs Γ₀(e) disc-count predictions.
refs: Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms (2002), ch. 12

title: LLL / Coppersmith small roots for ES Type I certificates at fixed p
connection: Coppersmith's method finds small roots of modular polynomials; Type I asks for f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p (mod 4cd), a small-root problem for a polynomial in (c,d) modulo an unknown divisor (Howgrave-Graham variant).
why: Turns certificate search into lattice reduction with provable size ranges; complements factoring-based search at 10^18–10^25.
first_step: Implement Howgrave-Graham's 'approximate common divisor / unknown divisor' lattice for N(c) = p² + 4c²d, d fixed, and compare its hit rate with brute force at p ~ 10^20.
refs: Coppersmith, Small solutions to polynomial equations, and low exponent RSA vulnerabilities, J. Cryptology 10 (1997)
Howgrave-Graham, Approximate integer common divisors, CaLC 2001

title: OAI 182 power savings for polynomial differences at primes (claimed)
connection: OAI 182 claims power-saving Sárközy-type bounds for differences P(p), p prime; ES certificate polynomials evaluated at primes are a polynomial-at-primes family.
why: Weak link; records that difference-set methods at prime arguments now have power savings.
first_step: Check whether any ES certificate condition is a 'difference set avoids P(primes)' statement; likely close.

title: Bhargava-style 'average over a family then sieve to the subfamily' for ES over n in APs
connection: Bhargava's method: count over a big family with geometry of numbers, then sieve to squarefree/maximal subfamilies via uniformity estimates; ES averaged over n in APs mod M is a sieve to sub-families.
why: Uniformity estimates ('tail' bounds) are exactly what pass from averages to subfamilies like Mordell-hard classes.
first_step: Compute averaged ES counts over n ≡ r (mod 840) for each Mordell-hard r and check uniformity in r of the main-term constant.
refs: Bhargava–Shankar, Binary quartic forms having bounded invariants, and the boundedness of the average rank of elliptic curves, Ann. Math. 181 (2015)

title: Linking form of the double branched cover of a 2-bridge link with a 3-vertex plumbing description
connection: L(p,A) is the double branched cover of the 2-bridge link b(p,A). The ES₅ sign is the isometry class of the linking form of Σ₂(b(p,A)), and HJ length 3 means a 3-vertex linear plumbing (negative-CF) description. Note this is not an 'even' continued fraction: three even HJ digits would give an even determinant.
why: Knot theory has exact formulas tying linking forms, Goeritz matrices and signatures (Gordon–Litherland). If σ mod 8 detects (A/p), the ES sign becomes a knot signature on a 3-parameter knot family.
first_step: Compute σ(b(p,A)) by Murasugi's formula Σ_{i<p} (−1)^{⌊iA/p⌋} for p < 500. Check whether σ mod 8, together with p mod 8, determines (A/p) (a van der Blij / Gauss-sum reciprocity).
refs: Gordon–Litherland 1978, On the signature of a link

title: Heegaard Floer d-invariants of L(p,A) as an obstruction/selector for 3-chain plumbings
connection: d-invariants of lens spaces satisfy an explicit recursion (Ozsváth–Szabó), d(L(p,q),i) via d(L(q, p mod q), j). Plumbing length 3 constrains the negative-definite fillings, and the ES sign is the homotopy class.
why: d-invariants are a native tool for deciding which lens spaces bound which definite 4-manifolds (Lisca's rational-ball classification itself used Donaldson's theorem and lattice embeddings; d-invariants give complementary obstructions). They might give a closed-form test of 'some 3-chain filling exists in the non-square class'.
first_step: Implement the Ozsváth–Szabó recursion. For p < 2000, compare Σ_i d(L(p,A),i) statistics over the classes A with r(p/A) = 3 between (A/p) = ±1.

title: Rational balls bounded by lens spaces (Lisca) vs 3-chain plumbings
connection: Lisca classified lens spaces bounding rational homology balls (p = m², specific q). Square p is exactly where ES-type certificates vanish (T1), and rational-ball bounding is tied to the linking form being metabolic.
why: T1 (obstruction at odd squares) and 'bounds a rational ball' are both 'linking form is split/hyperbolic' phenomena. A Lisca-style lattice-embedding argument could explain T1 topologically and show why primes escape it.
first_step: Read Lisca math/0701610 §§2–3 (lattice embeddings). Check whether the T1 square-class obstruction is equivalent to the metabolic linking form of L(m², A) for the relevant A.
refs: arXiv:math/0701610 (Lisca, Lens spaces, rational balls and the ribbon conjecture)

title: Lattice embedding of the 3-chain into the diagonal lattice ℤ^k (Donaldson-style)
connection: If a definite filling can be glued to another definite filling (of the reversed manifold) to give a closed definite 4-manifold, Donaldson's theorem forces the combined intersection lattice to be diagonal, so the plumbing lattice embeds in −ℤ^k (Lisca's method). For the chain (v,t,u), embeddings into ℤ^3 or ℤ^4 are explicit combinatorics, and the ES sign is a property of the complement lattice's discriminant.
why: This is the native toolbox of 4-dimensional topology for lens spaces, and it turns ES₅ into a finite combinatorial embedding question at each p.
first_step: Enumerate embeddings of chain lattices with det p into ℤ⁴ for p < 500; check whether the orthogonal complement's discriminant square class equals the ES sign.

title: Goeritz matrix of an alternating 2-bridge diagram equals the chain matrix
connection: For the plumbing description, the Goeritz form of a suitable 2-bridge link diagram should be (up to sign and stabilisation) the tridiagonal chain matrix (check the diagram convention: plumbing digits are not the same as twist-region counts of the standard diagram). Gordon–Litherland gives σ = sign(G) − μ.
why: This pins ES₅ to an explicit knot diagram: a 3-twist-region 2-bridge knot of determinant p. Knot tables could be scanned for the sign.
first_step: Check against KnotInfo: for 2-bridge knots with det p ≡ 1 (4), p < 200, and 3 twist regions in even CF form, record the linking-form class.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Quantum (WRT) invariants of lens spaces: Gauss sums carrying (A/p)
connection: Jeffrey's formula for the Witten–Reshetikhin–Turaev invariant of L(p,q) involves Dedekind sums and quadratic Gauss sums whose evaluation produces Jacobi symbols in q. The ES sign may appear as a phase of a quantum invariant of L(p,A).
why: Quantum topology has exact formulas (and quantum modularity results) for WRT invariants of Seifert/lens spaces. A sum over words of a quantum invariant could be a computable object.
first_step: Write τ_r(L(p,A)) (Jeffrey 1992). Check whether some level r makes the phase equal to (A/p), and evaluate Σ_{A ∈ L₃(p)} τ_r(L(p,A)).
refs: L. Jeffrey, Chern–Simons–Witten invariants of lens spaces and torus bundles (CMP 1992)

title: Hyperbolic triangle billiards / Veech triangles with prescribed area
connection: Billiards in the hyperbolic (π/x, π/y, π/z) triangle unfold to the triangle group's tiling of H² (not to Euclidean translation surfaces). Separately, Euclidean rational triangles unfold to translation surfaces, and Veech's lattice triangles are special shapes there. ES is a statement about the area spectrum of reflection-group triangles.
why: A genuine dynamics translation of the original equation, but probably only a restatement. Recorded for breadth.
first_step: Check whether the area/angle condition has any known role in Veech-group classification (Kenyon–Smillie, Ward triangles).

title: Ford circles: A/p lies in a horoball of 'depth-3' chain
connection: r(p/A) = 3 means the Ford circle chain from ∞ to A/p has three tangency steps of HJ type. ES₅ becomes: some non-residue A has A/p inside the union of depth-3 Ford horoball chains.
why: The Ford circle picture makes the condition a covering-by-horoballs statement, where hyperbolic volume arguments live.
first_step: Draw/compute the union of depth-3 HJ horoball chains intersected with {A/p}; measure its proportion and its correlation with QR.

title: Closed geodesic of γ_w on the modular surface: trace N−m and word length 3
connection: γ_w is hyperbolic when |A+A*| > 2. Its closed geodesic has a cutting sequence of length governed by the word. Prime geodesic theorems with Jacobi-symbol twists (Sarnak's class-number sums) count such objects.
why: Prime geodesic theorems in conjugacy classes and with characters are fully developed; ES₅ is a twisted count of geodesics with very short cutting sequences.
first_step: Write trace(γ_w) = tu + tv − 2 = A + A* and list the conjugacy classes; check whether ES₅ is equivalent to a short-cutting-sequence geodesic of trace in a given set with a character condition.
refs: Sarnak, Class numbers of indefinite binary quadratic forms (1982)

title: Toric degeneration of U_n to the torus complement xyz ≠ 0 and the Newton polytope
connection: As n varies, 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) degenerates (n → 0, n → ∞) to toric strata. Newton polytope methods (Bernstein–Kushnirenko, Khovanskii) count solutions in tori over finite fields; positive integer solutions relate to the polytope's interior lattice points.
why: Newton-polytope/tropical methods give exact solution counts over F_q (Ax–Katz divisibility of point counts) and might give mod-2 parity of solution counts.
first_step: Compute #U_n(F_q) exactly via the toric model and check Ax–Katz-type q-divisibility; record whether any parity information survives to positive integer points.

title: The lattice Λ_A = {(x,y) : y ≡ Ax (mod p)}: ES₅ ⇔ a non-residue A whose lattice has a short vector in a hyperbolic region
connection: vA ≡ u (mod p) with v | p+u means (v, u) ∈ Λ_A with uv small. By Minkowski every Λ_A has a vector with |x||y| ≤ p. ES₅ needs (v, u) with vA − u = p exactly (not just mod p) and positive.
why: It is geometry of numbers in its native form: minima of the family of lattices Λ_A over A ∈ QNR. Successive minima of Λ_A relate to CF data, with a Hecke-type averaging over A.
first_step: For p < 10⁵ compute λ₁(Λ_A) for all A and the minimum over non-residue A of the product-norm minimum; relate to λ(p).

title: Klein polygons / sails of the cone for p/A: HJ length = number of sail vertices
connection: The HJ digits of p/A are read off the boundary of the convex hull of the non-zero lattice points in the cone of the toric model of 1/p(1,A) (e.g. cone((0,1),(p,−A)) up to orientation convention; Klein's sail). The boundary lattice points are the HJ convergents (r(p/A) + 2 Hilbert-basis points), and geometric vertices are the points with digit ≥ 3. So r(p/A) = 3 means exactly 3 interior boundary points.
why: Arnold's statistics of sails and multidimensional continued fractions are a native toolbox. Sails with few vertices are rare and structured.
first_step: Express 'sail of cone(p,A) has 3 interior vertices' and count over A ∈ QNR; compare with Arnold's predictions for random cones.

title: Subconvexity for L(1/2, f × χ_{−4p}) and shrinking-target CM equidistribution
connection: Equidistribution of CM points in shrinking targets reduces (via Waldspurger) to subconvexity for twisted L-functions. ES certificates live in a target of measure ~p^{−1/2+o(1)}.
why: It gives the precise exponent gap: Weyl-strength subconvexity yields shrinking targets of size p^{−1/12}-ish, far from p^{−1/2}. It is a clean calibration.
first_step: Compute the target measure exactly, then the required subconvexity exponent; record the gap.
refs: Michel–Venkatesh, The subconvexity problem for GL₂ (Publ. IHES 2010)

title: Smith theory / ℤ/2-equivariant topology: fixed points of an involution on a ℤ/2-acyclic certificate complex
connection: Smith theory: an involution on a mod-2 acyclic finite complex has a non-empty mod-2 acyclic fixed set. A simplicial complex on solutions (or near-solutions) that is provably ℤ/2-acyclic, with an involution whose fixed points are certificates, would give existence.
why: It is the topological generalisation of 'odd number of fixed points', more flexible than plain parity because acyclicity can be proved by shellability or discrete Morse theory.
first_step: Define a complex on words of all p′ ≤ p (or on near-certificates) with faces from shared letters; compute mod-2 homology for small p.

title: Discrete Morse theory / matching on the poset of near-solutions
connection: Acyclic matchings on a poset (Forman) count critical cells, and Euler characteristic = alternating count of critical cells. If an ES-defined poset has Euler characteristic ≠ 0, a critical cell (certificate) must exist.
why: It is a combinatorial-topology tool that generalises sign-reversing involutions with a global acyclicity condition, a strictly richer version of the windmill route.
first_step: Define a poset of partial certificates (e.g. levels/divisor pairs ordered by divisibility) and compute its Euler characteristic as a function of p (small p).
refs: Forman, Morse theory for cell complexes (1998)

title: q-deformed rationals [p/A]_q (Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko) and Jones polynomials of 2-bridge links
connection: MGO's q-rationals have numerator polynomials with positive coefficients, which equal (up to normalisation) Jones polynomials of 2-bridge links (Kogiso–Wakui). The fan graph is the Tait graph, so the Jones polynomial is a Tutte specialisation. ES₅ concerns the class of A, i.e. which 2-bridge link has numerator p.
why: A root-of-unity specialisation detecting (A/p) would make the ES sign a quantum invariant with positivity structure (q-rationals), possibly giving inequalities.
first_step: Compute [p/A]_q numerators for p < 300 and evaluate at q = i, e^{iπ/4}, e^{2πi/8}; test whether any evaluation's phase equals (A/p) on words.
refs: Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko, q-deformed rationals and q-continued fractions (Forum Math. Sigma 2020; check)

title: Divisor class group of the toric ring k[σ^∨ ∩ M] ≅ ℤ/p and the canonical class: the sign as an Atiyah–Bott/Gorenstein index datum
connection: The cyclic quotient 1/p(1,A) has class group ℤ/p generated by a boundary divisor D₁. The canonical class K corresponds to −(1 + A)·[D₁]-type data, so the 'position of K in ℤ/p' is a quadratic-residue question about 1 + A or A.
why: Native singularity invariants (Gorenstein index, canonical class position) are computable and might rephrase the sign as 'K is a square multiple of a generator'.
first_step: Compute [K] ∈ Cl = ℤ/p for 1/p(1,A) and express its square class via A; compare with (A/p).

title: Banaszczyk transference / covering radius for BALANCED_LATTICE relation lattices
connection: BALANCED_LATTICE uses μ_∞(Λ) (covering radius) of relation lattices of small primes mod q. Banaszczyk's transference theorems tie covering radius to dual minima, and the dual minima correspond to characters that are nearly trivial on S.
why: It is the lattice-theory native tool and is already partly used; recorded for completeness. Sharper transference (Regev–Stephens-Davidowitz) could improve constants.
first_step: Check whether the R–SD reverse Minkowski / transference improvements change BALANCED_LATTICE's numerical thresholds.
refs: Regev–Stephens-Davidowitz, A reverse Minkowski theorem (Ann. Math. 2024; check)

title: Lattice-based crypto SIS/LWE hardness as a heuristic for certificate existence in relation lattices
connection: The relation lattice Λ_q(S) = {x : ∏ g_s^{x_s} = 1} is an SIS-type lattice. Its short vectors relate to subset products hitting targets. Crypto worst-case to average-case reductions say random such lattices have short vectors of predictable length (Gaussian heuristic).
why: Gaussian-heuristic predictions for short vectors give a model of certificate existence that respects lattice structure, more refined than Poisson.
first_step: Compare the Gaussian heuristic for λ₁(Λ_q(S)) with actual values for q < 10⁵, S = first k primes; quantify the deviation.

title: Braid group B₃ lift of γ_w and link invariants of its closure
connection: SL₂(ℤ) is a quotient of B₃ (B₃ → SL₂(ℤ), kernel generated by (σ₁σ₂)⁶). Lifting γ_w to a braid and closing gives a link L_w. Link invariants (signature, Jones at roots of unity) are then functions of the word.
why: It gives another topological carrier of words, different from the 2-bridge/plumbing one, with Burau/Jones machinery.
first_step: Lift γ_w via M(b) ↦ σ₁^b σ₂^{−1}-type words; compute the signature of closures for p < 200 and compare with the sign.

title: Torus-equivariant localisation: counting words as fixed points of a T-action on a toric variety
connection: Lattice points in a polytope count T-fixed points / sections of line bundles (Brion, Lawrence–Varchenko). Words at fixed t are lattice points on a hyperbola, not a polytope, but at fixed (t,u) the v-condition is linear: the union over (t,u) is a union of 1-dim lattice point sets in progressions.
why: Equivariant localisation gives exact counts with signs (via Brion's formula) and might give a closed form for weighted word counts.
first_step: Write Σ_{words} x^t y^u z^v as a sum of rational generating functions (Brion-type) for each (t,u) cone; examine the analytic structure of the full sum.

title: Minkowski question-mark function: ?(A/p) as a dyadic rational with prescribed run structure
connection: ?(x) maps the CF of x to a binary expansion with run lengths equal to the partial quotients. ES₅ asks for a QNR A whose ?(A/p) (or an HJ analogue) has a 3-block structure.
why: It gives a singular-measure (Minkowski measure) viewpoint: the set of A/p with short expansions is where ?-measure concentrates on few dyadic blocks. It is close to the Stern item but uses measure-theoretic tools.
first_step: Compute ?(A/p) for A ∈ L₃(p) and look for structure (e.g. ? values lie in a few dyadic intervals); compare QR vs QNR.

title: ES₅ for p ≡ 5 (8) vs p ≡ 1 (8): different native fields for the two classes
connection: The five-slice equivalence λ(p) ≤ 3 is stated for p ≡ 1 (8). For p ≡ 5 (8), (2/p) = −1 gives cheap certificates. In lattice/sandpile terms, p mod 8 is the Gauss-sum class (Brown invariant) of the discriminant form, so different topological constraints apply.
why: Splitting by p mod 8 is natural in every field (Arf invariant of knots with det p, Brown invariant of linking forms). The hard class p ≡ 1 (8) is where the Arf invariant of a det-p knot is 0.
first_step: Record the per-class status (which classes are trivial, by which certificate) and check whether p ≡ 1 (8) hard primes correspond to knots with Arf = 0 and signature ≡ 0 (mod 8).

title: Lens space surgery obstruction: QNR lens spaces are never integral surgeries on knots in S^3 (linking-form/homotopy obstruction)
connection: p-surgery on a knot K ⊂ S³ gives H₁ = ℤ/p with linking form ±1/p, so a lens space L(p,q) arising this way has ±q a square mod p. For p ≡ 1 (4) that means (q/p) = +1. Hence ES₅(p) ⇔ some lens space that is homotopically not an integral knot surgery bounds a 3-chain plumbing. Greene's solution of the lens space realisation problem uses exactly plumbing-lattice embeddings.
why: It locates the ES sign in a famous problem: Greene's lattice-embedding classification (via changemaker lattices) gives a complete description of the square class side. The ES side is its complement.
first_step: Read Greene (Ann. Math. 2013), §§1–3. Check whether the changemaker-lattice machinery has a version for the non-square linking class (e.g. surgeries on knots in other 3-manifolds) that yields 3-chain plumbings.
refs: Greene, The lens space realization problem (Ann. Math. 2013)

title: Quantum modular forms / Ẑ-invariants of the ES Seifert spaces
connection: WRT invariants and GPPV Ẑ-invariants of Seifert spaces with three exceptional fibres are false-theta functions, i.e. quantum modular forms (Lawrence–Zagier for the Poincaré sphere; Gukov–Pei–Putrov–Vafa). ES Seifert spaces M(0; 1/x,1/y,1/z) with e = −4/n form a family indexed by solutions.
why: Sum over solutions of a quantum invariant gives a generating object attached to n. Speculative, but it puts the solution set into an automorphic-adjacent structure different from Thm K.
first_step: Compute Ẑ (GPPV formula for Seifert spaces) for the ES Seifert spaces of small n and inspect the dependence on n.
refs: Gukov–Pei–Putrov–Vafa, BPS spectra and 3-manifold invariants (2017; check arXiv)
Lawrence–Zagier, Modular forms and quantum invariants of 3-manifolds (1999)

title: Gauss–Bonnet / area argument: hyperbolic area of the 'certificate horoball region' vs number of words
connection: In the closed-horocycle or Farey picture, words correspond to cusp regions whose hyperbolic area can be computed by Gauss–Bonnet. Total area ≈ count × typical area gives a geometric derivation of the log²p main term.
why: A geometric derivation might reveal a monotonicity or tiling argument (regions tiling a fixed area) that forces at least one word in each 'colour' region.
first_step: Compute the hyperbolic area of the union of HJ-length-3 regions at level p and check whether it is asymptotically a constant (tiling-type) or grows.

title: Thue's lemma / short vectors in lattices L_{p,λ} producing (★) triples
connection: Thue's pigeonhole gives |x|,|y| ≤ √p with x ≡ λy (mod p). Choose λ from ES structure (e.g. λ ≡ −4⁻¹ or ratios from Rat_e) and test whether short vectors produce positive (★) data.
why: Pigeonhole-in-a-box is the cheapest every-p mechanism; ES's linear congruence p ≡ −(u+B) (mod 4uB) has a modulus depending on the unknowns, so a 2-D lattice must be found for each candidate level.
first_step: For fixed C (or u), (★) says 4uC − 1 | p + u: build the lattice {(x,y) : x ≡ y·λ_C mod (something)} and check numerically whether LLL-short vectors give solutions.

title: Multiscale induction on level sizes
connection: Wang–Zahl proved 3D Kakeya by multiscale induction (sticky structure). ES certificates live at scales (C, u, B) with uBC ≈ p/4; formulate a statement S(X): 'every p has a certificate with C ≤ X or a structural reason to have one at scale X²' and attempt an induction on scales.
why: Scale induction is how several every-type geometric statements were proved recently; ES has a natural scale hierarchy.
first_step: From data, record for each p the smallest C with a certificate and the 'near miss' structure at smaller C; look for a recursive pattern across dyadic scales.
refs: arXiv:2502.17655 (Wang-Zahl, Volume estimates for unions of convex sets, and the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions)

title: Topological existence: Tucker/Ky Fan on a complex built from divisor lattices
connection: Lovász proved Kneser via Borsuk–Ulam; Tucker's lemma is its combinatorial form. Build a simplicial complex from divisor configurations of 4Cp+1 across levels with a free ℤ/2-action (d ↔ N/d swap or u ↔ B swap) such that an equivariant labelling without a 'complementary edge' is impossible, and complementary edges are certificates.
why: Topological methods give existence with no counting at all, immune to the polylog-main-term problem.
first_step: Toy version: for one level C, model divisors as vertices of a cross-polytope (±q_i) and check whether certificate-freeness defines an antipodal-free labelling; compute its index.

title: Weak subconvexity: ES needs only an ε-saving over the trivial bound R ≥ 0
connection: Soundararajan's weak subconvexity extracts a (log)^{−δ} saving from multiplicativity and mean values alone. ES: R = M_gen + X with X ≥ −M_gen trivially (R ≥ 0); ES is exactly 'X > −M_gen', any saving over the trivial bound. Seek a multiplicativity-driven argument producing X ≥ −(1 − δ)M_gen.
why: Frames ES as the weakest possible improvement over a trivial bound, the regime where 'soft' multiplicative arguments sometimes succeed.
first_step: Identify the multiplicative structure of the coefficients in X(p) (characters of order ≥ 3 mod 4uB evaluated at p) and test whether a Halász-type mean-value argument applies.
refs: arXiv:0809.1636 (Holowinsky-Soundararajan, Mass equidistribution for Hecke eigenforms)

title: Family of twists by characters mod p: R as a coefficient of a p-twisted object
connection: Subconvexity in the q-aspect uses the family of all characters mod q. ES at p involves characters mod p evaluated at small integers ((−m/p) in T(p)); consider the family {R_χ(p) : χ mod p} of character-twisted certificate counts and its moments, where orthogonality mod p is available.
why: The q-aspect family is the natural family for a fixed p (it does not need varying p), so moment methods apply without leaving p.
first_step: Define R_χ(p) = Σ_{certificates} χ(u)… for χ mod p; compute Σ_χ |R_χ(p)|² exactly by orthogonality and see whether it controls the trivial-character term.

title: Antipodal structure: the swap involution u ↔ B as a free ℤ/2-action on near-certificates
connection: Borsuk–Ulam/Tucker need a free ℤ/2-action. The (★) data (u, B) ↦ (B, u) is a ℤ/2-action, free off the diagonal u = B; certificates come in swap pairs (R(p) even). Study the ℤ/2-index of the space of near-certificates (a cell complex over levels) — a non-trivial index would force a fixed configuration, i.e. a certificate.
why: Uses a symmetry ES already has (R(p) even) in a topological rather than parity way.
first_step: Build a small complex for p ≤ 10³ (cells = near-certificates, faces = relaxations) and compute its ℤ/2-index.

title: Transfer statement D (from Mordell–Schinzel in Z[T]): any proof must be non-uniform in n
connection: Since ES is false over Z[T] (eventual positivity) at square classes, no argument that also works verbatim for 'polynomial n' can prove ES. Proof strategies must use a property of integers that fails for polynomials (e.g. archimedean size of specific values, primality, bounded height search).
why: A meta-filter for proof ideas: test each idea by asking whether it would also 'prove' ES over Z[T].
first_step: Add this filter to the evaluation checklist of later waves (not applied here per brief).

title: Does the Type I share fall with L(1,χ_p)? (k₁ responds more strongly than k₂)
connection: Across p ≤ 2·10⁵, k₁ has α ≈ −0.34 on log L(1,χ_p), k₂ only ≈ −0.20, so the Type I share k₁/(k₁+k₂) should decrease as L(1,χ_p) grows; at lcm(1..19)+1 the split is nevertheless typical (k₁/k₂ = 2.3).
why: If the share effect were strong, a proof strategy could split by the size of L(1,χ_p) (Type I when some small prime is inert, Type II otherwise); the residual k₁/k₂ correlation +0.70 and the lcm(1..19)+1 data suggest the effect is modest.
first_step: Fit k₁/(k₁+k₂) against log L(1,χ_p) at p ≤ 10⁷ windows and at pseudosquare primes.

title: Exceptions are about dispersion, not mean: squarefree-ES (mean 19.8) has 3 exceptions, 20/p (mean 26.4) has 60 still occurring at 9·10⁴
why: Families defined as a 'share' of all solutions (squarefree, lcm-closed, no-3) inherit U's tight distribution and have tiny exception sets; families defined by a multiplicative constraint (k | xyz, the (★) line) have heavy lower tails. For a proof, pick families of the first kind.
first_step: Measure the coefficient of variation of each family's count (residual after log p) and plot last-exception vs CV; test the predicted monotone relation.

title: Hardness vs the order of 10 mod p (decimal period) — category check
connection: Decimal period of 1/p is ord_p(10); a correlation would only reflect (2/p), (5/p) structure already captured.
why: Guards against 'recreational' fingerprints; if a residual correlation remains after controlling for (2/p), (5/p), that is a genuine surprise.
first_step: Partial Spearman of U-residual with ord_p(10)/(p−1) given (2/p), (5/p).

title: Polynomial recurrence selectors
connection: Ask whether a parameter sequence chosen by polynomial recurrence repeatedly enters a sufficient residue pattern.
why: Recurrence could replace an unstructured search if its visits can be made effective.
first_step: Choose one exact sufficient congruence pattern and compute visits of quadratic parameter sequences modulo its modulus.

title: CRT covering radius
connection: View simultaneous modular exclusions as a periodic subset of integers and ask about its largest parameter gap.
why: The largest gap directly measures how far an auxiliary search may have to travel.
first_step: For several small modulus sets, enumerate the allowed residues over one period and compute maximum gaps.

title: Epsilon-net search portfolios
connection: Ask whether a small portfolio can hit every sufficiently large witness set in a specified finite parameter universe.
why: An epsilon-net statement would be a finite search guarantee, not a proof for all primes without uniform hypotheses.
first_step: Define the witness-set universe for a bounded experiment and compare greedy nets with random samples.

title: Discrepancy-balanced family splits
connection: Color certificate families into two portfolios whose coverage counts stay close across sampled primes.
why: Balanced splits can reveal genuine diversity and create independent-looking diagnostic datasets.
first_step: Solve a small discrepancy-minimization problem on the family-prime incidence matrix.

title: Rewriting confluence
connection: Orient exact identity transformations and ask whether different reduction paths reach a common normal form.
why: Confluence would make duplicate removal and family comparison mathematically cleaner.
first_step: For a finite rule set, enumerate critical overlaps and check equality by cross multiplication.

title: Sylvester's 1880 sequence and Egyptian fraction 'denominator growth': why 3-term is the hard case
connection: Sylvester's greedy gives 4/n in ≤ 4 terms always; the gap between 4 (easy, greedy) and 3 (open) is the whole conjecture. Historically, similar 'one fewer term' gaps were closed by divisor-structure lemmas (e.g. Nagell's results on 2/n, 3/n).
why: Revisit how the k = 2 and numerator 2, 3 cases were resolved (they are theorems); the proof pattern for 3/n (always ≤ 2 terms? no: 3/n = 2 terms iff n has a divisor ≡ 2 mod 3; else 3 terms) suggests that ES is the first case where the 'iff' divisor criterion is not local — which is exactly Mordell–Schinzel. Document the exact historical sequence of results.
first_step: Search and read: Nagell 1922/23 on a/n = 1/x + 1/y; Mordell's chapter 30; list which cases (numerator a, k terms) are theorems and by what method.

title: Mordell's chapter 30 'the equation 4/n' — the discarded alternative parametrisations
connection: Mordell lists several families beyond the mod-840 ones and remarks on their limitations; the discarded families may be non-polynomial in disguise.
why: Primary-source check; the campaign cites Mordell via secondary literature.
first_step: Read Mordell ch. 30 fully; transcribe every identity and its residue class; compare with the repo's identity census (git grep -il 'identit' -- 'DISCOVERIES.md').

title: Meta: switch the primary object from 'f(p) ≥ 1' to 'the failure set F_K = {p : no certificate with parameters ≤ K}' and study F_K as K grows
connection: F_K is a well-defined, computable set for each K; ES says ∩_K F_K ∩ primes = ∅. The sequence F_K (density, structure, smallest elements, Legendre profiles) is a richer object than f(p) and directly mirrors 'squares + sporadic' phenomena (F_∞ ⊇ odd squares).
why: Reframing from 'count' to 'nested exceptional sets' matches how Rickards–Stange and HKRS state results and may expose structure (e.g. F_K is eventually a union of thin sets).
first_step: Compute F_K for K = 1..50 (parameter = c²d or C) on n ≤ 10⁶ (all n); plot density vs K; list the structure of F_50.

title: Mathematical-olympiad lens: known olympiad problems 'show 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z for n ≡ r mod m' and their solutions as identity sources
connection: Many olympiad/Putnam problems ask for specific residue classes (e.g. n ≡ 2 mod 3, n ≡ 3 mod 4); their solutions are identities already in Mordell's list, but the *techniques* (e.g. choosing x = (n+1)/2…) occasionally differ.
why: Cheap; the AoPS archive is searchable.
first_step: Search AoPS for 'Erdős–Straus' and '4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z'; collect all identities; diff against the repo census.

title: Terzi 1971 / Bernstein 1962: the 'all n ≤ 10⁸' era used a different parametrisation (4/n = 1/a + 1/b + 1/c with a | n…) — check for a mechanism not in Type I/II language
connection: Bernstein's Crelle paper 'Zur Lösung der diophantischen Gleichung m/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z' treats general m; his parametrisation for m = 4 may differ from Elsholtz–Tao's and contain additional identity families.
why: Primary-source check.
first_step: Obtain Bernstein, J. reine angew. Math. 211 (1962); transcribe parametrisation and identities.

title: Puzzle for people/MO: 'Show that for every prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) EITHER some p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4u) OR some pe + 1 has a divisor in its tied class' — the two-sided one-parameter statement as a self-contained elementary conjecture
connection: If the e-slice equivalence holds exactly (repo claims so), this two-sided statement IS ES for primes — but phrased with two one-parameter families of shifted integers, no x, y, z. The 409/2521 data show each side alone fails.
why: A maximally elementary, 'shifted-integer divisor' phrasing is the best bait for elementary number theorists and for olympiad-style insight; also a crisp statement for the Erdős problems site.
first_step: Pin down the exact tied class for the multiplicative side from the e-slice form; verify equivalence to ES for p ≤ 10⁴ by brute force; post.

title: Mechanical analogy: springs in series (compliance adds) and integer stiffness
connection: Springs in series: 1/k = Σ 1/k_i ↔ same algebra as resistors; equivalent reformulation.
why: Duplicate of resistor item in algebra but different community (mechanics puzzles); keep as outreach variant.
first_step: Combine with resistor outreach note (no separate work).

title: Meta: generate approaches by 'pairing barriers with escape hatches' systematically
connection: Each barrier theorem has stated scope; scopes have complements (hatches) ↔ enumerate hatch × thick-object pairs mechanically.
why: Systematic hatch enumeration guarantees coverage; G1 matrix is one instance.
first_step: Extract scope conditions from each barrier and generate the Cartesian product of complements; dedupe against repo memos.

title: Meta: ES-strength statements ranked by 'how much stronger than ES' — look for the weakest ES-implying statement
connection: I3_𝒞, (★)∪b=1, ES₅, … are ES-implying ↔ which is weakest (most likely provable) while still implying ES.
why: Explicit lattice of ES-implying statements by inclusion of certificate sets clarifies where to aim.
first_step: Make a Hasse diagram of the repo's ES-implying statements with their known failure sets (finite lists) — the weakest with no failures is the best target.

title: Bernstein 1962 (Crelle) polynomial families for 4/n as historical identity catalogue
connection: L. Bernstein's 1962 paper on m/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z (esp. m = 4) gives families of solutions ↔ repo's identity tables.
why: Cross-check that the repo's identity catalogue includes Bernstein's families; may contain families on non-residue-class sets.
first_step: Check whether 'L. Bernstein, J. Reine Angew. Math. 211 (1962)' is the right citation and extract its families.

title: Mordell's 'Diophantine Equations' (1969) chapter on 4/n: his stated obstructions and hopes
connection: Mordell's book section where the mod-840 reduction appears ↔ his remarks on why identities can't cover squares.
why: Primary-source check of the Mordell–Schinzel narrative; might contain an overlooked suggestion.
first_step: Read the relevant section of Mordell's book and record his remarks verbatim (with page).

title: Sylvester 1884 coin problem as the t = 1 ancestor of ES words: history link Sylvester ↔ Erdős–Straus
connection: Sylvester's Educational Times result (largest non-representable = uv − u − v) is the t = 1 case of the ES word shape tuv − u − v ↔ ES is a 'Sylvester-type' question about which primes are k-Frobenius numbers.
why: A historical bridge; the Frobenius-number literature (Ramírez Alfonsín's monograph) might have studied the inverse problem 'given n, find semigroups with g_k = n'.
first_step: Read Ramírez Alfonsín, 'The Diophantine Frobenius Problem' (OUP 2005) index for 'inverse problem' and 'k-Frobenius'; note any result on which integers are Frobenius numbers of 2-generated semigroups with multiplicity constraints.

title: Which integers are k-Frobenius numbers of ⟨u,v⟩ with k ≡ 3 (mod 4): a direct elementary question to post
connection: Restating (★) without Egyptian fractions: 'every prime p ≡ 1 (4) except 14 known ≤ 10¹⁰ is the largest integer having exactly 4C−1 representations by some coprime pair u,v'.
why: Semigroup/Frobenius community (e.g. García-Sánchez, Rosales, Ramírez Alfonsín) may recognise it; experts in that field are not in the ES network.
first_step: Draft a short note/MO post in Frobenius language with data, clearly marking that (★) is sufficient for ES but not equivalent (user approval before posting).

title: Odd unit-fraction solution counts and polynomial lower bounds
connection: The same MO answer cites a result giving a lower bound on the number of odd-denominator solutions for larger odd term counts, while exact counts remain unknown. This matches F04w/F12/F21/F22: a lower-bound count for constrained reciprocal representations but a gap to exact pointwise behavior.
why: The proof's construction of many solutions under a congruence restriction may transfer to lower bounds for ES representations in selected residue classes.
first_step: Read Chen–Elsholtz–Jiang, cited in the answer (arXiv:1108.6118), and extract its solution-generating operation; test whether it produces multiplicative families of ES triples.

title: Honda's count of tight contact structures on L(p,A): (v−1)(t−1)(u−1) for p/A = [[v,t,u]]
connection: Honda: the number of tight contact structures on L(p,q) up to isotopy is ∏(b_i − 1) over the HJ digits of p/q. So ES₅ words are lens spaces of order p with exactly three-factor tight counts in the non-square homotopy class, and I3 (letters ≥ 3) means every factor is ≥ 2.
why: Contact topology adds a natural weight (the tight-structure count) to each word. Weighted counts Σ_A ∏(b_i − 1)(A/p) might be more regular than plain counts (e.g. given by a Heegaard Floer formula).
first_step: Compute the weighted sum W±(p) = Σ_{A ∈ L₃(p), (A/p)=±1} (v−1)(t−1)(u−1) for p < 10⁵ and look for a closed form.
refs: Honda, On the classification of tight contact structures I (Geom. Topol. 2000)

title: Sparsity index: why binary Goldbach is stuck and ES is worse
connection: Binary Goldbach has a main term n/log²n among ~n terms and never got pointwise; ES has main term ≍ log²p among ≍ p log p 'trial events' (PARITY_AUDIT trial form).
why: Quantifies how far ES is from any problem ever upgraded; directs search to reformulations with denser events (fewer trials, larger main term).
first_step: Define sparsity = log(main term)/log(#trials) for each ES reformulation (★, b=1, ES₅, e-slice, I3 words) and tabulate; look for the least sparse one.

title: Gradient ladder: infinitely many → positive proportion → 100% → every, for ES sub-statements
connection: Hardy→Selberg→Levinson→Conrey climbed the ladder for zeros on the line. For ES sub-routes (e.g. 'certificate with C ≤ (log p)^A', 'Type II with u = 1'), place each on the ladder (infinitely many / positive proportion / 100% / every) to find the highest rung reachable for a restricted family.
why: Restricted families at '100%' rung are cheap wins; the transition points show which restriction kills 'every'.
first_step: Tabulate known/expected rungs for 10 restricted sub-routes using repo results and quick numerics.

title: Euler's false conjecture: an 'obstruction class' that turned out solvable
connection: Euler believed n ≡ 2 (mod 4) had no orthogonal Latin squares; only 2 and 6 fail. Mordell-hard square classes look like an obstruction class for identities, yet ES holds there numerically. BSP's recursive constructions crossed the class barrier — look for recursive (product) constructions for ES certificates that move from easy classes into square classes.
why: Product/recursive constructions are exactly what identities (polynomial in p) cannot do; ES(n) ⇒ ES(kn) is a product construction but goes the wrong way.
first_step: Search for constructions producing certificates for p from certificates for auxiliary integers in easy classes (e.g. via the e-slice N = (p+e)/4 structure).

title: Reduction theory for ES solutions and congruence exclusion of all reduced representatives
connection: In Ghosh–Sarnak failures every orbit has a reduced representative in a bounded region, and congruence conditions can exclude all of them. ES: every solution has x ∈ (p/4, 3p/4] (x minimal); the 'reduced representatives' are the pairs (x, m = 4x − p). Ask whether congruence conditions modulo a fixed M can exclude all reduced representatives for infinitely many p (that would be a non-BM obstruction).
why: A concrete search space for genuinely new obstructions; if impossible for structural reasons, that fact is itself a (small) theorem.
first_step: For M = 840·k, compute which residues of p mod M admit a reduced representative whose two-term remainder is locally solvable mod M; check that no non-square class is fully excluded.
refs: arXiv:1706.06712 (Ghosh-Sarnak, Integral points on Markoff type cubic surfaces, Invent. Math. 229 (2022))

title: ES is false in a model of open induction (via Mordell–Schinzel in a discretely ordered ring)
connection: Discretely ordered rings like Z[T] with T infinitely large (and Shepherdson-type models of IOpen built from Puiseux polynomials) are models of weak arithmetic. ES in Z[T] with this order is the eventual-positivity polynomial world, where Mordell–Schinzel rules out n = mT + r².
why: Would show ES is unprovable in open induction, so any proof needs induction on non-open formulas — a precise statement about the logical strength of ES proofs (it is Π₁, so true-if-unprovable in PA).
first_step: Check that a suitable ring (e.g. Shepherdson's model, or Z + T·Q[T] variants) satisfies IOpen and that the Mordell–Schinzel argument applies there (denominators may have rational non-constant coefficients).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES in models of IΔ₀: does bounded arithmetic prove 'almost all n'?
connection: Vaughan's density theorem uses analytic number theory; formalizing it in weak arithmetic is unlikely, but elementary 'almost-all' proofs (sieve-free covering arguments) might live in IΔ₀ + Ω₁.
why: A weak-arithmetic analysis isolates which tools are logically necessary, e.g. whether exponentiation (power ladders) is needed.
first_step: Survey: is there any Erdős–Straus-type density statement formalized in bounded arithmetic? (Probably not — low priority.)

title: Ultraproduct of Z/pZ? No — ultraproduct of Z[1/S_k] with growing S: ES transfers by Łoś
connection: Since ES holds over every Z[1/ℓ] (odd ℓ < 3000 checked), it holds in ultraproducts of these rings; but these ultraproducts are not Z. Łoś only transfers first-order sentences true in almost all factors, giving nothing for Z.
why: A clean negative showing that proved S-integer worlds cannot transfer to Z by compactness; useful to prune approaches.
first_step: Record the negative; double-check that 'positive' is first-order definable in Z[1/ℓ] (it is, via sums of four squares).

title: Computability world: ES for 'computable reals'/Turing degrees — category error check
connection: Considered: 'ES over computable reals' is meaningless (no integrality). Kept only the meaningful variant: ES restricted to n in a decidable set is decidable for each n, and the set of ES-failures is co-c.e.
why: Confirms nothing beyond the Π₁ item; record to avoid revisiting.
first_step: None (closed).

title: Greedy-in-a-different-order world: choose z first (largest), then solve the 2-term problem
connection: Reverse greedy: pick z among divisors-structured candidates and check if 4/p − 1/z is a 2-term sum. Different search orders define different canonical solutions and different 'certificate complexity' measures.
why: If some order gives bounded search depth for all p tested, it suggests the right certificate measure for a proof.
first_step: Implement reverse search with z ∈ {p·d : d | small numbers} and measure depth needed for p < 10^6.

title: Hilbert's 10th / Diophantine sets: the set of ES-failing n is Diophantine (co-r.e.) — trivial but formal
connection: {n : ¬ES(n)} is Π₁-definable, hence its complement {n : ES(n)} is Diophantine (Σ₁) by MRDP; a polynomial whose positive values are exactly ES-good n exists. Nothing new arithmetically, but gives a 'polynomial certificate world'.
why: Mostly formal; MRDP polynomials are huge. Recorded to close the logic direction.
first_step: Note; skip unless a logician collaborator is interested.

title: Feature: independence of witness events
connection: Dividing-line feature 'independence of witness events'. ES UNCLEAR: certificate families share the integer p, correlations not controlled. To supply it one could: measure empirically the pairwise correlation between Type I families (a,d) and (a',d') as events over p, and bound them by large-sieve arguments
why: Crocker-type failures exploit strong correlation; Poisson heuristics need weak correlation.
first_step: Compute the covariance matrix of the 50 most frequent certificate families over p ≡ 1 mod 24 ≤ 10^7.

title: Feature: unbounded constructive case analysis
connection: Dividing-line feature 'unbounded constructive case analysis'. ES LACKS a known digit/recursive construction. To supply it one could: design recursive constructions driven by p's base-b digits or CF expansion of a/p (as palindrome theorem)
why: Cilleruelo–Luca–Baxter proves a pointwise result by an explicit algorithm with finitely many local rules applied unboundedly.
first_step: Check whether B1 (no finite ET covering) forbids digit-recursive constructions or only fixed-modulus coverings.

title: Independence heuristic predicts unbounded Vmin; data show a plateau at 116 — test it
connection: If fail_v events at a prime were independent with P(fail_v) ≍ C_v(log p)^{−1/2}, the probability that all v ≤ 116 fail is tiny but the number of primes is huge; compute the expected number of primes ≤ X with Vmin > 116 under the model and compare with 0 observed.
why: A discrepancy would quantify positive dependence/repulsion between shifts (FRONTIER's joint-failure discussion) using a sharp observable.
first_step: Use the single-shift law constants from EXSET_SHIFT_DIVISORS §2 to compute E#{p ≤ 3·10⁶ : Vmin(p) > V} for V = 31, 87, 116.

title: Logarithmic weights tuned to rare witnesses
connection: Weight certificates by divisor size or auxiliary complexity to reduce domination by primes with many easy witnesses.
why: A better weight may make sparse cases more visible in moment calculations.
first_step: Compare unweighted counts with reciprocal-divisor and inverse-multiplicity weights on the same prime sample.

title: Base-digit automata
connection: Track a certificate equation digit by digit with carries in a fixed base.
why: Polynomial equalities admit finite carry descriptions under bounded-width restrictions, yielding concrete restricted models.
first_step: Build a base-two carry checker for bounded denominator triples and minimize its state graph.

title: Automatic pattern diagnostics
connection: Test whether experimentally observed family selectors have low-complexity digit behavior.
why: A short automaton would suggest a recursive selector, though finite data cannot establish automaticity.
first_step: Infer minimal automata from initial selector labels and test them on a disjoint larger range.

title: Weighted automata for word height
connection: Add costs measuring coefficient size or word length to the congruence automaton.
why: Shortest accepted paths can find economical candidate certificates while respecting exact finite-state constraints.
first_step: Run shortest-path search with logarithmic coefficient cost and compare candidates against direct enumeration.

title: Synchronizing words for congruences
connection: Ask whether a shared suffix of elementary operations sends many residue states into a useful target set.
why: Such a suffix would be a reusable congruence repair mechanism, if allowed moves preserve the needed algebra.
first_step: Enumerate short suffixes in the modular transition system and measure the size of their target preimages.

title: Carry cellular automata
connection: View the multiplication and addition in the cleared ES equation as local carry interactions on digit strings.
why: Local update rules may reveal impossible digit patterns or efficient branch propagation.
first_step: Implement a bounded-width carry propagation diagram for a toy prime and compare its pruning with naive digit search.

title: Quantifier elimination for fixed ansatzes
connection: Use real or Presburger quantifier elimination only on subproblems whose language genuinely fits those methods.
why: Exact parameter-region descriptions could simplify one family without pretending general nonlinear integer arithmetic is decidable.
first_step: Choose a linear-congruence ansatz and eliminate one bounded parameter using a Presburger tool.

title: Algorithmic simplicity of difficult instances
connection: Compare the shortest known certificate-generating program with the smallest numerical certificate.
why: A huge denominator might still have a simple recurrence description, suggesting a different notion of difficulty.
first_step: For a small set of large-height examples, search short recurrences generating their denominator triples.

title: Arithmetic-circuit complexity
connection: Compare expanded polynomial identities with compact straight-line arithmetic circuits.
why: A low-complexity circuit may expose composition structure that expansion obscures.
first_step: Represent three candidate families as circuits and count multiplication gates after common-subexpression elimination.

title: Positivity proof certificates
connection: Attach explicit positive-factor decompositions to every symbolic denominator expression.
why: An algebraically correct identity can still fail as an ES construction if denominators are nonpositive.
first_step: For three candidate formulas, rewrite each denominator into products or sums whose signs follow from stated hypotheses.

title: Presburger/automatic-sequence test: is the set of (p, C_min(p)) k-automatic in any base?
connection: Automatic sequences and k-regular sequences are decidable by Walnut; if the first winning C (or Type I minimal c) were k-regular in p, Walnut could *prove* ES in that regime. Almost certainly not, but the negative result would be informative: it shows ES is 'non-automatic' which rules out all finite-automaton covering proofs.
why: Cheap and decisive one way or the other; connects to B1 in automaton language.
first_step: Compute C_min(p) for p ≤ 10⁶, test for 2-/3-/10-regularity with a k-kernel rank test (compute subsequences C_min(k^e p + r) and check linear dependence).
refs: Shallit, 'The Logical Approach to Automatic Sequences' (Walnut)

title: Decidability frontier: ES as a Π₁ sentence of bounded-quantifier arithmetic — is it provable in IΔ₀ + exp?
connection: ES is Π₂ (∀n ∃x,y,z) but with the bound x,y,z ≤ n² (true for ES? solutions can be bounded by n² in Type II forms? check) it is Π₁ with bounded search. Reverse-mathematics / bounded-arithmetic questions: which fragment proves the known partial results (Mordell identities are in IΔ₀; Vaughan's sieve needs exp).
why: Proof-theoretic strength calibration tells what style of argument can possibly work: if ES is provable in IΔ₀+Ω₁ then there is a 'polynomial-size certificate' explanation, which constrains the proof shape.
first_step: Check whether there is always a solution with max(x,y,z) ≤ n² (compute for n ≤ 10⁵; known bounds for Type II give z ≤ ...). Then search 'Erdős–Straus bounded arithmetic' / 'unit fractions IΔ0'.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0331] Write one paragraph documenting the logical strength landscape (ES ∈ Π₁; conservativity of ACA₀/WKL₀ over PA/IΣ₁ for Π₁ statements).

title: Kolmogorov complexity of the solution 'script' (c,d,f) across primes
connection: For each p, encode the lexicographically first Type I/II solution as a string; measure compressibility across consecutive primes (gzip of the concatenation, or a learned model's perplexity). Low complexity = hidden rule.
why: Direct test for 'there is a simple hidden rule the campaign has not found'. Cheap.
first_step: Produce the (c,d,f) first-solution sequence for p ≤ 10⁶, compress with xz/zpaq, compare with compressibility of a surrogate random sequence with the same marginals.

title: Streaming/sketching: minimal information about p needed to construct a solution
connection: Communication-complexity framing: Alice knows p mod M, Bob knows ⌊p/M⌋; how much communication is needed to agree on an ES solution? If O(1) bits suffice for some M, that's a covering system; if Θ(log p), solutions are 'global'.
why: A clean quantitative version of 'ES is not local' (Mordell–Schinzel says polynomial-local fails; this asks for any protocol).
first_step: Empirically: for M = 840, compute for each residue class r the size of the smallest 'dictionary' of solution templates (c,d) needed to cover all primes ≡ r up to 10⁶; growth with the range.

title: Compressed sensing / sparse recovery: f(p) as a sparse combination of character sums
connection: Express f(p) (or its Type I part) as Σ_χ c_χ χ(p) over characters of various moduli (it's not periodic, but truncated versions are); sparse recovery finds the dominant characters. Dominant terms = the identities that matter most.
why: Quantifies 'how periodic is f(p)' beyond Mordell's mod 840; a sparse spectrum would suggest a near-covering.
first_step: Fit f(p) − A log²p on p ≤ 10⁷ against characters mod M ≤ 10⁴ with LASSO; list top characters.

title: Grover-style amplitude amplification is irrelevant, but the quantum query lower bound technique (adversary method) applies to classical 'how many C must be tried'
connection: Adversary bounds give lower bounds on queries needed to find a winning C against a worst-case p; translated classically: any proof that tries C in a fixed order needs ≥ max C_min(p) cases.
why: Makes precise that a 'list of templates' proof must have unbounded length — reinforcing Mordell–Schinzel from an algorithmic angle, but also showing adaptive proofs are not bound by it.
first_step: Just note it; verify unboundedness of C_min(p) numerically (if C_min were bounded a finite cover would exist — contradiction with Mordell–Schinzel only for polynomial covers; so unbounded C_min is a separate empirical question!). Compute max C_min(p) for p ≤ 10⁸.

title: Adaptive C-choice using the factorisation of the previous failure: C_{k+1} = a prime factor of 4C_k p + 1
connection: If q | 4Cp+1 then 4qp·(something)... consider C′ = Cq: 4Cqp + 1 ≡ 1 − q·(4Cp) ... hmm; since 4Cp ≡ −1 mod q, 4Cq'p+1 for C' = C·k ≡ 1 − k mod q. Choosing k ≡ 1 mod q gives q | 4C'p+1 again with a different cofactor — a way to 'reuse' a prime factor q and search the cofactor's residue. This builds chains of C sharing factors: a tree search with algebraic guidance.
why: Algebraically guided chains may hit −1 mod 4C' faster than blind enumeration; and chain structure might be provable (like Euclid's algorithm steps).
first_step: Implement the chain rule and measure chain length to success vs C_min for p ≤ 10⁶.

title: Model theory: is ES expressible in a decidable theory after fixing the structure of (ℕ, +, ·|_{divisors of 4Cp+1})?
connection: Full arithmetic is undecidable, but fragments like Presburger + 'is a power of 2' (Büchi) or Skolem arithmetic (ℕ, ·) are decidable. ES mixes + and · minimally: 4Cp + 1 = ab, a ≡ b ≡ −1 (4C). Determine the weakest theory in which ES is expressible and whether any known decidability/undecidability result applies to its ∀∃ fragment.
why: Calibration: if ES lies in a decidable fragment, there's an algorithm to decide it (in principle); more realistically it identifies ES's logical complexity relative to e.g. Zaremba (also ∀∃ with bounded searches).
first_step: Write ES in the language (ℕ, +, ·, <) and try to reduce the number of multiplications; note that 'a ≡ −1 mod 4C' and 'ab = 4Cp+1' need two products with shared variables; check against the known decidable fragments (e.g. 'one multiplication' theories are already undecidable? — Robinson).
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0328] Read Lipshitz 'The Diophantine problem for addition and divisibility' and check whether ES(p) (with xyz multiplication eliminated via Type II linearisation) fits into the decidable fragment — and what the decision procedure's 'local-global' principle says.

title: Cellular automaton / tag system: encode the greedy-with-backtracking search for 3-term representations as a CA and study its space-time diagram for structure
connection: Rule-based searches sometimes reveal structure via their space-time diagrams (Wolfram's approach); the ES search tree over (x, y) with the two-term test is such a rule system.
why: Recreational/experimental; cheap; near-zero prior of a breakthrough but a possible visual hint.
first_step: Implement and plot for p ≤ 500; stop if nothing visible.
refs: Wolfram, A New Kind of Science

title: Kolmogorov complexity argument: a counterexample p would be 'simple'?
connection: Incompressibility method: if every p ≤ X of high complexity has a certificate, counterexamples must be low-complexity ↔ disproof search direction.
why: Adversarial searches already target structured p; formalising 'low complexity' (short description) to prioritise searches is a meta improvement.
first_step: Rank candidate primes by description length (e.g. p = a·b^k + c with small a,b,c) and search ES hardness there first.

title: Quantum algorithm: Grover search for certificates and complexity of certification
connection: Grover gives √ speedup for unstructured search ↔ ES certificate search space ~ p log p trials, polylog winners.
why: Not a proof route; clarifies computational complexity of finding a certificate (classical best ~ ?).
first_step: Determine the best classical algorithm complexity for finding one ES solution for a given p (repo/verification code) and record whether it's polylog-time heuristically.

title: Shor-type period finding: ES certificate as a hidden-subgroup instance?
connection: HSP over (ℤ/N)^× ↔ ES gate: subgroup generated by divisor classes containing −1.
why: Curiosity mapping; might reveal that certificate-finding reduces to factoring 4Cp+1 (which it does) — so ES search ∈ BQP-easy given factoring.
first_step: Write explicit reduction: ES(p) certificate search ≤ factoring of numbers 4Cp+1 for C ≤ polylog — then note quantum polynomial time.

title: Witnessing theorem contrapositive: if certificate-finding is hard (e.g. needs factoring), ES is not provable in weak arithmetic
connection: Divisor-form certificates need factoring 4Cp+1 ↔ if every certificate search needs factoring, ES ∉ provable in S¹₂ (under crypto assumptions).
why: Gives a meta-theorem: proofs must use non-constructive or strong tools; clarifies why elementary attempts fail.
first_step: Check whether ES certificates can be found without factoring (e.g. via the Type I trial form, which needs only divisibility tests, poly-time per trial). If yes, the obstruction vanishes.

title: Program synthesis: search for a short program f(p) → (x,y,z) correct for all p ≤ 10⁸
connection: Program synthesis (e.g. enumerative, stochastic superoptimisation, LLM-guided) ↔ a uniform algorithm with provable termination would be ES.
why: Any synthesised program with a bounded loop is a finite menu (B1, must fail i.o. under Dickson); but unbounded-loop programs with simple invariants could suggest a proof structure.
first_step: Run a DSL search (loops over small parameter, modular tests) for programs certifying all primes ≤ 10⁶ with minimal description length; inspect top programs for invariants.

title: Automata: is the set of p (in base b) with a certificate of size ≤ B a regular language? (Büchi/Cobham)
connection: Sets defined by finitely many congruence conditions are b-automatic ↔ finite menus give automatic sets; ES (all primes) is not automatic but the complement of a finite menu is.
why: Cobham's theorem: automatic in two multiplicatively independent bases ⟹ ultimately periodic. Menus are periodic; any 'digital' certificate rule (digit-carry algorithms, B1 hatch) gives automatic sets in one base only — a way to classify digit-based ideas.
first_step: Take a digit-carry ES rule (repo E2 hatch) and compute its automaton; check whether its success set is periodic (then B1) or genuinely base-dependent.

title: ECM-style randomised factoring of 4Cp+1 tuned to divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C
connection: ECM finds small factors; ES only needs some divisor in a class ↔ certificate search at astronomical p.
why: Engineering: lets adversarial searches reach p ~ 10^100 cheaply (only smooth parts needed).
first_step: Implement: for C ≤ 10⁴, pull small factors of 4Cp+1 by trial division/ECM and test subproducts for class −1 mod 4C; measure success rate at p ~ 10^100.

title: Satisfiability modulo theories with nonlinear integer arithmetic: prove 'ES for n ≡ r mod M' identities automatically
connection: SMT (Z3 NIA) can verify polynomial identities with divisibility ↔ automatic discovery of Mordell-type identities for new classes (non-square).
why: Automated rediscovery of all identity classes mod larger moduli maps exactly which classes have identities (Mordell–Schinzel says square classes never do).
first_step: Use a template x = (a n + b)/c etc. and let a solver search coefficients making 4/n = … an identity on a residue class mod 4·k; enumerate classes covered mod 9240.

title: Hash-based birthday search for collisions between Type I and Type II slices
connection: Birthday paradox: two large lists collide ↔ ES via matching a Type I partial with a Type II partial (meet-in-the-middle).
why: Meet-in-the-middle reformulations sometimes convert existence into collision guarantees (G1 collision column).
first_step: Find a decomposition ES(p) ⟺ L1(p) ∩ L2(p) ≠ ∅ with |L1|,|L2| ≍ √p range; test sizes and collision counts.

title: Kolmogorov–Arnold / sparse regression on Fourier coefficients of 1[R(p) small]
connection: Fourier analysis over (ℤ/M)^× of the indicator of hard primes ↔ which characters correlate with difficulty.
why: Large Fourier coefficients identify characters (e.g. quartic residue symbols) beyond quadratic ones that influence R(p).
first_step: Compute Σ_{p hard} χ(p) for all characters χ mod M ≤ 10⁴ (normalised) and list outliers.

title: Compactness argument: ES holds for all n iff a certain closed subset of Ẑ contains no positive integers
connection: The set of n ∈ Ẑ not covered by ET identities is closed ↔ positive integers in it must be handled by non-identity (non-local) certificates.
why: Formalising this would define the 'global part' of ES precisely as integers in a profinite closed set (squares in Ẑ are in it). Then ES ⟺ integer points of that set (non-squares) each have a large certificate.
first_step: Define precisely: K = Ẑ minus ∪(open ET identity classes). Compute K ∩ (ℤ/M) projections for M up to 10⁶; check whether K equals the closure of squares or is larger.

title: Ultraproduct / nonstandard primes: a nonstandard counterexample p* in an ultrapower
connection: If ES is true, it's true in all models of PA where it's provable; a nonstandard model with ES failing at a nonstandard p* would show independence from weaker systems.
why: Model-theoretic view: properties of p* (e.g. p* ≡ square mod every standard m ⟹ p* a 'locally square' prime) mirror sterile points; a structural link between nonstandard counterexamples and profinite sterile points.
first_step: Write: p* nonstandard with no standard-size certificate ⟺ p* ∈ K (sterile set) for all standard moduli ⟹ p* is locally a square at all standard primes? Check logically.

title: Overspill: if every prime ≤ N has a certificate of size ≤ (log p)^A, by overspill some nonstandard N too — useless direction; reverse: underspill for counterexamples
connection: Overspill/underspill principles ↔ bounding certificate size uniformly.
why: Mostly logical hygiene: shows 'uniform polylog bound' and 'ES' are equivalent in nonstandard terms only with explicit bounds.
first_step: Skip unless pursuing logic angle; first step: write a paragraph mapping ES's bounded-quantifier form to overspill.

title: Fibonacci's Liber Abaci methods for Egyptian fractions as algorithm catalogue
connection: Fibonacci gave several decomposition rules besides greedy ↔ alternative constructive rules for 4/p.
why: Each rule is a candidate certificate family; testing coverage is cheap.
first_step: List Fibonacci's seven rules (via Sigler's translation / Dunton–Grimm summary) and test each as 4/p → 3 terms.

title: Local-global principle for systems of linear divisibilities (Lipshitz/Bel'tyukov)
connection: Existential (ℤ,+,|) theory satisfies a local-global principle: a system of divisibilities among linear forms is solvable iff solvable mod all primes powers (with conditions) ↔ ES Type II: (4uC − 1) | p + u is a divisibility between non-linear forms; but u fixed gives linear in C.
why: If ES (or a sufficient condition) could be phrased as a system of linear divisibilities with finitely many unknowns, a local-global principle would decide it — and locally ES is always solvable!
first_step: Find: with u fixed as a parameter, is '∃C: (4uC − 1) | p + u' a linear divisibility system? It is: ∃C,k: k(4uC − 1) = p + u — non-linear (kC). Search for a linear-divisibility sufficient condition, e.g. '∃C: (4C − 1) | (p + 1)' (u=1): linear in C! Then local-global says solvable iff locally solvable — but local solvability of 4C − 1 | p + 1 as C varies ⟺ p+1 has a divisor ≡ 3 mod 4 … check the theorem's precise statement (it may need the divisor to be a linear form in the variables on both sides).

title: Hilbert's 10th problem over ℤ with divisibility: Diophantine definability of 'has a divisor ≡ −1 mod m'
connection: The predicate D(N,m) = ∃d | N, d ≡ −1 mod m is existential ↔ complexity of deciding ES-type predicates.
why: Logical classification only; supports TFNP items.
first_step: Note D(N,m) is in NP (certificate d) and coNP? (unknown); state as complexity question.
